title: Productivity and Growth
short: Output per hour of work rises with physical capital, human capital and technology.
trouble: Students credit growth to more hours of work alone, and miss that lasting gains in living standards come from more output per hour.

blocks.html: Over decades, Nominal and Real GDP per person has risen many times over in the richest countries. That is growth of the economy's capacity, the outward shift of the production possibilities curve. Where does it come from?

Labor productivity is real output per hour of work. Real GDP = output per hour × hours worked, so real GDP grows by about the growth of productivity plus the growth of hours. Lasting gains in living standards come from productivity, which rises with physical capital (machines, buildings, equipment), human capital (skills and education) and technology (better ways of producing).

More hours of work raise output, but there are only so many hours in a week, and more work means less leisure. Output per hour has no such limit. A worker with a better tool, more training, or a smarter method produces more in the same hour. Capital alone runs into diminishing returns: the tenth machine per worker adds less than the first. Technology lifts the whole relationship, so the same capital and skills produce more. That is why economists see new ideas as the deepest source of long-run growth.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: An aggregate production function, with capital per worker $k$ across the bottom. Move along the curve: each extra unit of capital per worker adds less (diminishing returns). Raise $A$ (technology): the whole curve lifts.

blocks.title: Output per hour
blocks.q: A country produces \$12,000 billion of real GDP with 200 billion hours of work. Find labor productivity.
steps: $\dfrac{12{,}000 \text{ billion}}{200 \text{ billion hours}} = 60$ dollars per hour.
Each hour of work produces \$60 of real output on average.

blocks.title: Splitting growth
blocks.q: Productivity grows 2% a year and hours grow 1% a year. How fast does real GDP grow? How much of it raises output per hour?
steps: Only the 2% from productivity raises output per hour, the part that lifts living standards.

Example
rows: faster trucks, robots on an assembly line, new office buildings
a welding course, more students finishing college
a cheaper way to make solar panels, better software
blocks.cap: The three sources of productivity growth.

blocks.html: Crediting growth to more hours of work alone, and missing that lasting gains in living standards come from more output per hour. Check: divide output by hours; if output per hour is flat, people are richer only because they work more.
